summary: Argues for standard host names for Telnet and recommends four-character names, with eight-character alternatives, for the hosts then on the network. Each host was expected to suggest its own call letters. Names would be case-insensitive.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 233 proposes short symbolic names for hosts in Telnet programs. It gives four-character and eight-character choices and recommends that uppercase and lowercase letters work the same way.

questions: what host call letters did rfc 233 recommend
subtitle: A proposal for short host call letters in Telnet programs.

tldr.problem: The authors saw value in standardizing symbolic host names used by Telnet programs.
tldr.mechanism: They recommend that hosts suggest call letters of four characters, with eight-character alternatives, and that letter case be interchangeable.
tldr.outcome: The RFC publishes a recommended list of names for the hosts then known to the authors.

today: RFC 233 is a host naming proposal published in September 1971. The unit metadata lists its status as Unknown.

sections.title: Why Standardize Host Names
sections.content:
The authors agree that standard symbolic host names would benefit Telnet users. They note a trade-off between brevity and names that help users remember a host, and argue that a useful set can fit within four characters.

They recommend that each host suggest its own call letters and that uppercase and lowercase be treated interchangeably.
sections.plainLanguage: Standard names could make hosts easier to identify in Telnet. The authors want short names but also recognize that a memorable name can be longer.

sections.title: Recommended Host List
sections.content:
The RFC lists host numbers alongside a four-character name and an eight-character name. Examples include sex and sex-ucla, nic and nic-sri, and ucsb in both columns.

The list represents the authors' current recommendations; the RFC does not define a mechanism for automatically distributing or updating the names.
sections.plainLanguage: The table pairs host numbers with shorter and longer names. Each site was expected to suggest its own call letters.

sections.title: Case Handling
sections.content: The proposed names use letters in a way that permits upper- and lowercase forms interchangeably. This is the only explicit operational rule in the RFC beyond the recommended name lengths and list.
sections.plainLanguage: A user could enter a proposed host name in uppercase or lowercase. The RFC recommends that both forms identify the same name.
